questions.q: In the real pytest run shown in this lesson, why did `assert result[0] == 0.1` fail even though `pct_returns` was computing the correct value?
options: Because pytest cannot compare floats at all
Because 110.0 / 100.0 - 1.0 produces 0.10000000000000009, not exactly 0.1, due to IEEE-754 floating-point representation -- the test's exact-equality assertion was wrong, not the code
Because the array had the wrong dtype
Because pct_returns had an off-by-one bug
questions.explain: The real failure output showed `assert 0.10000000000000009 == 0.1` -- the computation was correct, but exact float equality is the wrong assertion to use, which is exactly what this lesson's fix (pytest.approx) addresses.

questions.q: What is the correct fix for comparing a computed float to an expected value in a test?
options: Round both values to the nearest integer before comparing
Use a tolerance-based comparison like `pytest.approx` or `np.testing.assert_allclose` instead of `==`
Avoid testing any code that uses floating-point arithmetic
Convert the float to a string and compare strings
questions.explain: pytest.approx (for scalars) and np.testing.assert_allclose (for arrays) compare within a tolerance, which is the correct approach for floating-point results that may differ in the last few bits depending on computation path.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend explicit tests for edge cases like empty arrays and NaN propagation, rather than relying only on 'normal case' tests?
options: Because pytest requires at least 5 tests per function

Because numerical code commonly works correctly on the normal case seen during development but mishandles empty inputs, NaN propagation, or overflow in ways that only an explicit test for that case will catch
Because NaN values are always bugs and should never appear in test data
Because empty arrays always cause a Python syntax error
questions.explain: The lesson identifies empty inputs, NaN propagation, and overflow as recurring sources of silent numerical bugs that normal-case tests don't exercise -- hence the need for dedicated tests like test_pct_returns_empty_array and test_pct_returns_with_nan_propagates.

questions.q: What does a `hypothesis` property-based test check, that a hand-written example-based test does not?
options: It checks that the code runs faster than a specified threshold
It checks that a general rule (a 'property') holds across many automatically generated inputs, rather than just the specific examples a developer thought to type by hand
It checks that the code has no syntax errors
It replaces the need for any assert statements
questions.explain: In the real example, @given(positive_prices) caused hypothesis to generate many different price lists and verify the length-matching property held for all of them, catching cases a fixed set of hand-picked examples might miss.

questions.q: In the real hypothesis test run described in this lesson, what property was being verified by `test_pct_returns_length_property`?
options: That all returns are positive
That the length of the returned array always equals max(len(prices) - 1, 0) for any generated list of positive prices
That pct_returns never raises an exception
That the returns are always sorted in ascending order
questions.explain: The test asserted `len(result) == max(len(prices) - 1, 0)` for every generated price list, which is the structural property pct_returns should satisfy regardless of the specific input values or length.
